Chart system concept 02

Register

Register leads with the numbers. Every chart sits in the same frame, so a reader learns its parts once, and every chart carries a register: the figures a reader would look up, set in a table under or beside it.

Other views: Newsprint · Charcoal · Social card · System

How to read our charts
  1. The label says what kind of evidence a chart holds: a Finding is measured; an Estimate depends on stated assumptions.
  2. The title is the claim. “Would” and “may” mark claims that are less sure.
  3. The measure line says what was counted, where and when, and whether the scale starts above zero.
  4. The darkest ink marks what the title names; gray gives context.
  5. The register and notes print every number and say what the chart leaves out.
  6. Red marks the single point a title names, when a chart uses it. Red never means a party, good or bad.

The full guide is on the System view, section 8.

Chart system concept 02 · Register

Social card

Chart S01 as a portrait post at 1080 by 1350 pixels, the size Instagram and LinkedIn use. It is live type at true size, so the box below scrolls on a phone. The card keeps the frame: evidence label, title, measure line, the party register, the dated votes and the full source line.

Other views: White · Newsprint · Charcoal · System

Alt text for the exported image

A card from Oath & Action. Finding: Nearly nine in ten Republicans and Democrats favored a ban on stock trading by members of Congress. Bars show 88 percent of Democrats, 87 percent of Republicans and 86 percent of all registered voters, from a survey fielded May 19 to 30, 2023. The House passed a ban, H.R. 7008, 232 to 198 on July 22, 2026; on September 30 the Senate voted 53 to 47 to take it up, short of the 60 votes, three-fifths of the Senate, needed to end debate. From Who Do They Answer To?, the Oath & Action systems atlas.

Rules for cards

  • Type keeps its system roles at card size: label 26 px, title 60 px, figures 68 px, party names 32 px, votes 28 px, source 20 px.
  • The source line prints whole on the card itself.
  • Party rows share one ink and print the party name.
  • The card names Oath & Action and the atlas; it carries no web address until the site is settled.
  • The wordmark sits at the foot; it is the only red on the card.

Chart system concept 02 · Register

The system on one sheet

The rules a designer or a builder needs to make the next chart: the frame and its parts, the type, the marks, the palettes with measured contrast, the table rules, notes and sources, red, and the guide for readers.

Other views: White · Newsprint · Charcoal · Social card

1The frame

Studio note · not part of the chart

S03 Ranked bar

Reader questionWho changed the rules: voters, courts or legislatures?

Why this formA ranked register answers “who” by grouping the instruments by who acted; each glyph in a bar is one change, and the direction columns read across a row and down a column.

Every figure uses the same ten parts in the same order, so a reader learns them once.

  1. Rule2 px Charcoal across the figure. It opens every figure and nothing else on the page uses it.
  2. Evidence labelInter 700, 13/18, capitals, 0.06em. The kind (Finding, Association, Estimate, Illustration), then a few words on where the numbers come from.
  3. TitleInter Tight 800, 28/32 (22/27 on phones). A sentence that states the finding, with a verb that matches the grade.
  4. Measure lineInter 400, 15/23, Deep Stone, at most 75 characters a line. Measure, unit, place and period; a cropped scale is said here.
  5. FigureThe chart or the register. Artboards at 866, 560, 358 and 328 px, each shown at its own size, so nothing scales.
  6. Note in the drawingInter 400 or 600, 13/16, with a ground-colored halo, joined to its data by a 1 px leader that crosses no series.
  7. NotesInter 400, 14/20, Deep Stone, numbered, 45 to 75 characters a line. What a reader needs to read the figure fairly; then the coding rule and the disclosure where the data needs them.
  8. Source lineInter 400, 13/18, Deep Stone. Publisher, table, period, place, date retrieved, qualification. The credit “Chart: Oath & Action” and the link to the reading guide sit beside it.
  9. Table“Show the S0n table”: every value, every note and the source, readable by a screen reader.
  10. Studio noteDashed box beside the figure, used in the guide only.

Grid: 12 columns at 1440 px with 64 px margins and 24 px gutters; the figure takes 866 px and the studio note the rest. On phones, 16 px margins, one column, the figure first.

The kit: every chart comes from a generator that takes rows, and the frame, the register generator and the chart tokens are shared. A drawing that puts a line through a word, or a label outside its box, stops the build.

2Type

Locked faces only: Inter Tight for titles and big figures, Inter for everything else, Lora Italic for quoted words only. Every number is tabular, every minus is the true minus (−), quotes and apostrophes are curly, dates print in words, and nothing falls under 13 px.

3Marks

  • Bars start at zero; in-row bars share one scale per table, and every bar’s value is printed.
  • Lines may start above zero only when the measure line says so. Missing years and method changes break the line.
  • Points sit on one straight scale per panel. Small multiples share one scale.
  • One mark per record: squares toward voters, dots away from voters, hollow squares for no change, hatched for mixed, dashed for pending. Units are 14 px; in a register bar each glyph is one change.
  • Gridlines are horizontal hairlines on the half pixel, with no ticks; the baseline at zero is Charcoal.
  • Every label in a drawing carries a ground-colored halo, so a gridline never runs through a word.
  • Charts do not move. A later animated chart starts with a reduced-motion path that shows its final state.

4Palettes, measured

Lab values come from the shared palette lab; Register’s own tints (the quiet rule, the map tint and the Verdigris lift on Charcoal) are mixed in OKLab from locked colors, each with one job. Contrast is WCAG 2 against the ground. Marks that carry meaning clear 3:1. Light fills inside a scale (the plausible and contested grades, the map tint, the light diverging steps) sit under 3:1 only where every value prints in the register or the table, a design judgment. In a contrast theme a tint never carries meaning that its glyph or its printed value does not also carry.

The direction pair, Verdigris squares and Charcoal dots on White, differs by OKLab distance 0.370 (0.364 under deuteranopia, 0.386 under protanopia, 0.371 under tritanopia), and by shape. Neither is Prussian or red. Stone and Verdigris never separate two categories alone.

Diverging scales never pair red with blue. Register tests candidate B, Prussian through the ground to Verdigris, in S06; candidate A, Stone through a neutral to Verdigris, stays with the other concepts for Gate 2. No state map and no direction code uses Prussian, so a blue mark never reads as a party.

5Tables

  • Numbers sit right-aligned in tabular figures, with one count of decimals per column, so the decimal points align.
  • A change column prints its sign: +0.2, −3.7. Zero prints as 0 in Deep Stone; a missing value prints as words.
  • Column heads carry the unit, once: “Documented, %”. Rows carry no unit.
  • Rules stay quiet: Charcoal under the head, a quiet tint between rows, Stone above a group, Charcoal above the total.
  • The default sort answers the question: ranked by value, grouped by who acted, or by date. Long tables let a reader re-sort.
  • A bar inside the row, 12 px high, shows the shape; the printed figure carries the value. Bars stay visible in Windows contrast themes.
  • On a phone each row reflows into labeled lines, so no table scrolls sideways.
  • Group and total rows carry their own counts in bold, and they sum.

6Notes, sources and fairness

  • A note inside the drawing does one job: names the record, explains an odd encoding, or gives a reader’s scale.
  • Join a note to its data with a 1 px leader or a bracket. Never hide a note behind hover.
  • Notes under the figure say what the reader needs to read it fairly: revisions, breaks, coding rules, margins of error, and the editor’s disclosure on charts about the rules his campaigns concern.
  • Notes, measure lines and sources run 45 to 75 characters a line. Reader-facing words name no colors and no source codes.
  • Before a title ships, read it once as a reader on the left and once as a reader on the right.
  • Label illustrative items beside the item. Titles say what the evidence supports and nothing more.

The source line keeps section 15 order. Shorten it only by dropping words; every fact stays.

  1. PublisherU.S. Census Bureau
  2. Title or tablePoverty in the United States: 2025 (P60-290), Table 8
  3. Observation period2009 to 2025
  4. GeographyUnited States
  5. Date retrievedRetrieved November 6, 2026
  6. QualificationFigures for 2019 to 2024 include the Bureau’s August 2026 revision

7Red

“The wordmark’s ampersand and the lockmark’s lever are signature red and do not count, and neither do the ampersands inside the hinge diagram and the hinge-circle badge, which are identity marks. The hinge diagram never shares a view with the wordmark and never stands in for the hinge divider. An icon’s red accent counts as signature red when the icon stands alone, as an app tile, an avatar or a single feature icon. In a row or a menu, icons go one color and only the current one keeps its red. Each view (one screen, card, slide or printed page) then carries one working red, in this order of precedence: an error the reader must fix; the step a reader can take now; the one point the headline names, which in a systems figure is where a reform acts. One job may take several marks, such as each target of one reform. A hinge headline’s ampersand uses the view’s working red. The hinge divider’s ampersand takes its surface’s ink: Charcoal on Newsprint and White, Newsprint on Charcoal, White on Prussian. In the guide itself, specimens, labeled failure cases and palette swatches do not count. Red never sits on Prussian.”
Rule 05.3 (D2-01)

On a chart page red never encodes a series, a category, a grade or a scale. It may mark the one point a title names, and only when no error or ask holds the view’s red. A chart posted alone may mark the point its title names in red; a chart added to a page takes red only when the page’s red job moves to it. The chart views of this page carry no working red. The two drawings below are guide specimens, so their red does not count.

8How to read our charts

For readers, printed once in a report and linked from every chart.

  1. Start with the label. It names the kind of evidence. A Finding is a measured result with a source and a period. An Association is a pattern that does not show cause. An Estimate is a modeled value that holds only if its stated assumptions do. An Illustration uses made-up numbers to show how a chart works, and says “Illustrative data” beside it.
  2. Read the words after the label. They say where the numbers come from. “Official statistic” is a figure a government agency publishes; “self-reported” is what survey respondents said; “documented” means on the public record; “a secondary list” was compiled by someone other than the original source.
  3. Read the title as the claim. Its verb says how sure the evidence is: words such as “passed”, “fell” or “ban” for documented facts; a plain statement for well-supported findings; “can” or “may” for plausible ones; “would” for estimates that hold only if their assumptions do; “untested” for a hypothesis; and both readings where the evidence is contested.
  4. Check the measure line. It says what was counted, where and when, and whether the scale starts above zero.
  5. Find the darkest ink. It marks the series or the point the title names; gray gives context. A chart with its own code, such as the evidence grades, says so in its key.
  6. Know what red means. When a chart uses red, it marks the single point the title names. Red never means a party, good or bad.
  7. Allow for survey error. Survey numbers come from a sample of people, so each has a margin of error. A margin of 0.5 points means the true figure most likely sits within half a point either way, and a smaller change may be chance.
  8. Know what “the atlas” is. Who Do They Answer To? is Oath & Action’s own research record of the rules. Charts drawn from it say so, and the directions they show are its codes, printed under the chart.
  9. Look up the numbers. The register under each chart prints the figures, and “Show the table” holds every value, note and source.

Data: Oath & Action, Who Do They Answer To? Systems Atlas V7, snapshot of October 15, 2026; U.S. Census Bureau tables retrieved November 6, 2026; Ballotpedia, retrieved November 6, 2026. Every source line sits under its chart.
